title: Throughput budget and thresholds runbook for enterprise GPU proposals
content:
Purpose:
This working runbook is intended to be a lightweight, reproducible playbook we can use when drafting enterprise deployment proposals that involve reserved GPU capacity. It is focused on: throughput budgeting (tokens/sec and requests/sec), autoscaling thresholds and policies, and a simple GPU cost estimator so we can produce fast, defensible numbers for customers.

Audience & context:
- Solutions engineers drafting committed-capacity proposals for enterprise customers who require predictable latency and cost (e.g., chat assistants, retrieval-augmented applications, batch embeddings).
- Assumes customer wants a ded­i­cated pool (reserved) with canary/bursting behaviors to hosted variants.

High-level workflow (how to use this doc):
1) Collect workload profile from customer: typical request size distribution, peak requests per minute (RPM), target p95 latency, concurrency expectations, and tolerance for fallbacks.
2) Select candidate model family and quantization level (FP16, int8/4).
3) Estimate per-request GPU duty cycle using tokens/sec or sequence length distribution and batching assumptions.
4) Produce conservative capacity estimate (min GPUs) + autoscaling thresholds + burst buffer.
5) Run sensitivity analysis (±20–50% traffic, cache hit rates 0–60%).
6) Deliver proposal with recommended committed units, expected monthly GPU-hours, and worst-case cost.

Step 1: Workload signals to capture (ask these of the customer)
- Request rate: average and 95th/99th percentile RPM for production windows.
- Sequence length distribution: median / p90 / p99 in tokens. If unavailable, sample from logs or instrument a short traffic replay (1–2 hours).
- Response payload size: tokens returned per request (important for KV cache reuse).
- Arrival pattern: steady vs bursty (diurnal spikes, campaign-driven surges).
- Latency SLOs: target p50/p95/p99 for user-facing endpoints.
- Acceptable fallbacks: degrade to smaller model / hosted fallback?

Step 2: Per-request GPU time model (one-line approximation)
- Base formula: GPU_time_per_req = (in_tokens + out_tokens) * cost_per_token_ms(model, hw) / batch_efficiency_factor
- Derive cost_per_token_ms from our internal perf bench for model+hw at target sequence lengths (use nearest bucket).
- Batch_efficiency_factor depends on average effective batch size (empirical from workload mix).

Example calculations (concrete):
- Customer: enterprise chat, p95 RPM peak = 300 RPM (5 RPS), sequence distribution median 120 tokens in / 60 tokens out, p95 512 in / 256 out.
- Model: open-llama-like medium; on A100-40GB FP16 bench: cost_per_token_ms ≈ 0.9 ms/token single-stream baseline. For quantized int8 on H100 variant assume ~0.6 ms/token.
- Choose conservative bucket: 0.9 ms/token.
- Average tokens/request = (120 + 60) = 180 tokens. GPU_time_per_req ≈ 180 * 0.9 ms = 162 ms.
- If average effective batch size = 6 (dynamic batching), batch_efficiency_factor ≈ 0.6 (we get ~40% speedup per token). Adjusted GPU_time_per_req ≈ 162 ms * 0.6 = 97 ms.
- Throughput per GPU = 1 / 0.097 s ≈ 10.3 req/sec.
- For peak 5 RPS sustained -> 1 GPU could handle 10.3 RPS. Add buffer: recommended >= 1.5x -> 1.5/10.3 ≈ 0.15 GPUs -> round up to 1 GPU. For p95 larger sequences, re-calc and you may need 2 GPUs.

Guardrails & conservative knobs:
- Always compute with p95 sequence lengths for capacity commit. Use median for baseline autoscale sensitivity testing only.
- Add a 20–50% headroom multiplier to throughput requirements for enterprise SLAs and network variance.
- Prefer fractional math but commit in integer GPU units; express burst as autoscale/burst policy to avoid overcommit.

Autoscaling policy template (recommended defaults for dedicated pool):
- Metric: GPU_utilization_average (per-pool) and request_queue_length (per-replica). Use both metrics in policy.
- Scale-up triggers:
  - If request_queue_length > 5 for 30s OR GPU_utilization_average > 72% for 60s -> add one replica (GPU).
  - If p95_latency_experiencing_growth: if p95(latency) > SLO * 1.2 for 60s -> immediate +1 GPU and alert.
- Scale-down triggers:
  - If GPU_utilization_average < 30% for 5m AND request_queue_length == 0 for 2m -> remove 1 replica (graceful drain).
  - Minimum pool size = committed_reservation (do not scale below contracted GPUs).
- Burst policy:
  - Allow ephemeral burst to hosted pool when local capacity exhausted and customer allows fallback. Configure fallback policy with max burst duration (e.g., 5 minutes) and cost cap.

Operational notes for autoscale tuning:
- Use sample intervals >= 30s to avoid reaction to microbursts; use an ephemeral short window for queue-length to respond faster to sudden demand.
- Tie scale-up to queue growth more aggressively than utilization because utilization can be misleading when KV cache hits reduce compute.
- Implement a cooldown of 3–5 minutes between successive scale actions to avoid flapping.

Cost estimator quick recipe (monthly GPU-hours):
1) Compute required GPUs = ceil(peak_req_per_sec / per_gpu_req_per_sec * headroom_multiplier).
2) Monthly GPU-hours = required_Gpus * 24 * 30 * utilization_factor (utilization_factor accounts for reserved vs actual use, suggested 0.75 for steady workloads).
3) Monthly GPU cost = monthly_GPU_hours * hourly_cost_of_GPU (use committed discount rates).
4) Add platform + networking + storage overheads (rough rule: +12–18% of GPU cost).

Cost example (following previous calculation):
- From throughput calc, conservative required GPUs at p95 = 2 GPUs. Headroom_multiplier = 1.3 -> required_Gpus = ceil(2 * 1.3) = 3 GPUs.
- Monthly GPU-hours = 3 * 24 * 30 * 0.75 = 1620 GPU-hours.
- If committed A100 discounted rate = $2.75/hr (example), GPU cost = 1620 * $2.75 = $4,455.
- Platform + infra = 15% -> +$668; total ~= $5,123 / month.
- Present two alternative scenarios (cheaper quantized model or higher traffic) in proposal.

Sensitivity scenarios to include in customer-facing appendix:
- Traffic +30%: GPUs -> ceil(2.6*1.3)=4, hours -> 2160, cost -> +33%
- KV cache hit 40%: effective token work down 40% -> GPUs drop from 3 to 2 in many cases
- Model quantized int8: per_token_ms drops 25–40% -> GPUs drop proportionally

Fallback and graceful degradation strategies to propose to customer:
- Automatic fallback to smaller model variant on sustained p95 breach (with quality degradation warning).
- Partial response mode: return summary-only for very long responses to reduce output tokens.
- Queue shedding: For extreme overloads, use token-budget-based circuit (e.g., limit requests above X tokens during burst windows).

Runbook: emergency scale-up (play-by-play):
- Step 0: Alert fires: p95 latency sustained > 1.2*SLO for 60s. Pager on-call SE and SRE.
- Step 1: Check pool metrics: replica health, queue_length, GPU_utilization.
- Step 2: If autoscaler not responding, manually add 1 replica and enable burst to hosted fallback.
- Step 3: Validate tail-latency improvement in 60–90s. If no improvement, add another replica and review logs for hot-shards or model OOM.
- Step 4: Post-incident: capture traces, correlate to upstream traffic, recommend increasing committed base if incident caused by sustained load.

Proposal template snippet to share with customers (short):
- What we recommend: commit to 3 A100-equivalent GPUs (reserved) for baseline production with autoscale to 5 (ephemeral) and hosted-burst fallback configured up to 10 RPS for 5 minutes.
- Why: This configuration meets p95 latency target under expected p95 sequence lengths with 30% headroom for campaign traffic.
- Monthly cost estimate: $~5.1k (committed) + monitoring and support (listed).
- Sensitivity: +30% traffic increases cost ~33%; enabling int8 quant reduces cost up to ~25–35%.

Open questions / follow-ups before finalizing a proposal:
- Can customer accept hosted fallback for bursts or do they require absolute on-prem capacity?
- Are there predictable campaign windows we should model separately?
- Can they provide a 2–4 hour traffic sample for more precise batching/latency sims?
- Any security constraints that mandate isolating logging/traces (affects cost and storage).

Attachments / quick references (internal):
- perf-bench table ids: bench-2024-q3-a100-llama-medium, bench-2024-q2-h100-quant.
- Useful JIRA filters: SE proposals in last 90d (jira:filter/SE-commitments).

Last notes (practical heuristics we use):
- When uncertain, bias toward too-small committed size but larger burst allowance; this keeps up-front cost low while protecting customer UX via controlled fallbacks.
- Document the assumptions clearly in the customer proposal (sequence length distribution, batch size, latency SLO). If assumptions change, rerun the model and rebaseline the commitment.

Author: Arjun Patel (solutions engineering) — working draft for internal review.
summary: Working runbook for estimating GPU capacity, autoscaling policies, and cost scenarios for enterprise dedicated deployments; includes formulas, example calculations, autoscale templates, runbook steps, and follow-ups.
